title: A Phone Call Is All It Takes: How "Pink" Is Draining Microsoft 365 Accounts and Extorting SMBs

html:
A new threat group is bypassing your MFA, emptying your OneDrive, and sending ransom demands from your own employees' accounts. It all starts with a phone call.

The group, tracked as "Pink" (CL-CRI-1147) and believed connected to the broader Com criminal network, launched a dedicated data leak site on May 31, 2026. Their method isn't malware. It isn't a phishing link. It's a voice call.

How the Attack Works

An employee receives a call from someone claiming to be IT support. The caller is convincing. They know the company name, they reference a real-sounding ticket or security alert, and they direct the employee to a credential-harvesting site with a name designed to look legitimate: passkeyaddcom, passkeydeploy.com.

The employee enters their Microsoft 365 credentials. Game over — almost.

MFA should stop this. It doesn't. Pink doesn't need your password after this point because they steal your active login session. The authentication token is already valid. MFA has already been passed. The attacker is now inside your Microsoft 365 environment as you.

From there, they use Microsoft's own automation tools to extract files from OneDrive and SharePoint at speed. No suspicious executables. No malware signatures to detect. Fileless execution inside legitimate system paths, running in temporary memory, with sandbox detection to avoid analysis environments.

Then comes the demand. Not from an unknown attacker address but from your own employee's compromised account, via email and Microsoft Teams. 72 hours to pay. Your own colleagues receive the extortion message.

Why This Attack Succeeds

The technical sophistication is real, but the entry point is entirely human. Every component after the phone call is automated and fast. The bottleneck is the first 30 seconds of that call.

Three things make employees vulnerable:

Urgency framing. IT calls that open with "we've detected unusual activity on your account" trigger compliance, not skepticism. The instinct is to fix the problem, not interrogate the caller.

Legitimate-looking domains. Passkeydeploy.com doesn't look like a phishing domain at first glance. It sounds like something an IT department would use. Domain lookalike monitoring catches registrations like this but only if you're watching.

MFA false confidence. Employees who know MFA exists often believe they're protected even if they hand over credentials. Session hijacking renders that assumption wrong.

What Relay Shield Detects

This attack chain, it has detectable signals at two points:

Before the credential harvest: Domain lookalike monitoring flags newly registered domains mimicking your company or your software vendor, often within hours of registration, before the phishing campaign goes live. Passkeydeploy.com was registered ahead of the campaign. A monitored domain watchlist would have surfaced it.

After the credential harvest: Infostealer and breach monitoring flags your employee email addresses the moment credentials appear in underground markets or known breach databases. If an employee's session was stolen and their credentials extracted, that exposure surfaces giving you a response window before the attacker acts.

The vishing call itself is harder to detect in advance. What you can control is the response protocol. RelayShield's /vishing command delivers a step-by-step verification protocol your team can follow when an unexpected IT call arrives: callback verification, credential request red flags, and how to report suspicious calls before entering anything.

What to Do Right Now

If your business runs Microsoft 365:

Brief your team on callback verification: Any unexpected IT call requesting credentials should be verified by hanging up and calling your IT contact directly on a known number.

Monitor for domain lookalikes of your company name and your key software vendors (Microsoft, your MSP, your bank).

Check whether your employee emails have appeared in breach databases: If so, compromised credentials from prior breaches are often the starting point for targeted vishing campaigns.

Review active Microsoft 365 sessions: Under your account settings, active sessions should reflect only devices and locations you recognise.

The 72-hour deadline Pink imposes is designed to prevent exactly this kind of methodical response. Preparation before the call is the only defence that works.
